'''Roman Wladimir Jackiw'''{{efn|{{langx|uk|Роман Володимир Яцків|{{transliteration|uk|ukrainian|Roman Volodymyr Yatskiv}}}}}} ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|r|oʊ|m|ɑː|n|_|ˈ|dʒ|ɑː|k|iː|v}}; {{IPA|pol|ˈrɔman ˈjakʲiv|lang}}; November 8, 1939 – June 14, 2023) was an American theoretical [[physicist]] and [[Dirac Medal (ICTP)|Dirac Medal]]list.

==Early life and education==
Jackiw was born in [[Lubliniec]], [[Poland]], in 1939<ref>{{Cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=REcOAQAAMAAJ&q=%22Jackiw,+Roman%22+1939 | title=Encyclopedia of Ukraine| last1=Kubiĭovych| first1=Volodymyr| last2=Struk| first2=Danylo Husar| year=1984| publisher=University of Toronto Press| isbn=9780802034441}}</ref> to a Ukrainian family that moved to Austria and Germany before settling in [[New York City]] when Jackiw was about 10.<ref>[https://repository.aip.org/jackiw-roman-2010-august-5 Oral History Transcript — Dr. Roman Jackiw] [[American Institute of Physics]] (5 August 2010)</ref>

Jackiw earned his undergraduate degree from [[Swarthmore College]] and his PhD from [[Cornell University]] in 1966 under [[Hans Bethe]] and [[Kenneth G. Wilson|Kenneth Wilson]]. He was a professor at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] [[MIT Center for Theoretical Physics|Center for Theoretical Physics]] from 1969 until his retirement. He retained his affiliation in [[emeritus]] status in 2019.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://web.mit.edu/physics/people/faculty/jackiw_roman.html |title=MIT Department of Physics Faculty |website=[[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] |access-date=16 July 2019}}</ref>

== Career ==
Jackiw co-discovered the [[chiral anomaly]], which is also known as the Adler–Bell–Jackiw anomaly. In 1969, he and [[John Stewart Bell]] published their explanation, later expanded and clarified by [[Stephen L. Adler]], of the observed decay of a neutral [[pion]] into two [[photon]]s. This decay is forbidden by a symmetry of [[classical electrodynamics]], but Bell and Jackiw showed that this symmetry is not preserved at the quantum level. Their introduction of an "anomalous" term from [[quantum field theory]] required that the sum of the charges of the elementary [[fermion]]s be zero. This work also gave important support to the color theory of [[quark]]s.

Jackiw is also known for [[Jackiw–Teitelboim gravity]], often abbreviated as '''JT Gravity''', a theory of gravity with one dimension each of space and time that includes a [[dilaton]] field. Sometimes known as the '''''R'' = ''T'' model''', it is used to model some aspects of near-extremal [[black hole]]s.<ref>{{cite arXiv |eprint=1907.03363 |last1=Stanford |first1=Douglas |last2=Witten |first2=Edward |authorlink2=Edward Witten |title=JT Gravity and the Ensembles of Random Matrix Theory |date=7 July 2019|class=hep-th }}</ref>

== Personal life ==
{{Unreferenced section|date=January 2026}}
Jackiw married fellow physicist [[So-Young Pi]], daughter of Korean writer [[Pi Chun-deuk]]. Jackiw's sons are the violinst [[Stefan Jackiw]] and Nicholas Jackiw, a software designer known for inventing [[The Geometer's Sketchpad]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Sketchpad Story - The Geometer's Sketchpad Resource Center |url=https://www.dynamicgeometry.com/General_Resources/The_Sketchpad_Story.html |access-date=2026-02-20 |website=www.dynamicgeometry.com}}</ref> His daughter, Simone Ahlborn, is an educator at [[Moses Brown School]] in Providence, Rhode Island.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-06-22 |title=Farewell to the Master of Quantum Puzzles: MIT’s “Giant of Theoretical Physics” Roman Jackiw Dies at 83 |url=https://scitechdaily.com/farewell-to-the-master-of-quantum-puzzles-mits-giant-of-theoretical-physics-roman-jackiw-dies-at-83/ |access-date=2026-08-27 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-06-20 |title=Professor Emeritus Roman Jackiw, “giant of theoretical physics,” dies at 83 |url=https://news.mit.edu/2023/roman-jackiw-giant-theoretical-physics-dies-0620 |access-date=2026-08-27 |website=MIT News {{!}} Massachusetts Institute of Technology |language=en}}</ref>

Jackiw died on 14 June 2023, aged 83.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://physics.mit.edu/news/in-memoriam-roman-jackiw-jerrold-zacharias-professor-of-physics-emeritus-1939-2023/ |title=In Memoriam: Roman Jackiw, Jerrold Zacharias Professor of Physics Emeritus (1939-2023) |first1=Deepto |last1=Chakrabarty |website=MIT |date=June 15, 2023 |access-date=June 17, 2023}}</ref>
